reason: Supported by multiple independent sources detailing the Vela Pulsar's extreme physics, discovery history, and the live radio recording of its spin glitch.
story: One thousand light-years away, a dead star collapsed into an ultra-dense sphere just 12 miles wide, spinning over eleven times per second. Born in a massive supernova over ten thousand years ago, the Vela Pulsar sweeps violent radiation jets across deep space like a cosmic lighthouse. But this dead star has a terrifying habit: every three years, it glitches. Without warning, the pulsar suddenly violently speeds up its spin. In 2016, astronomers monitoring the Mount Pleasant Observatory caught a glitch live for the very first time. Right as the star glitched, it skipped a beat entirely, missing a pulse before snapping back to speed in just five seconds. Scientists believe this violent hiccup happens when the pulsar's churning superfluid core suddenly grips its solid outer crust, transferring energy and revealing the extreme interior physics of one of the universe's deadliest engines.
angle: A dead star spinning 11 times a second suddenly 'glitched' and missed a pulse live on radio telescopes as its liquid core grabbed its outer crust.

claims.claim: The Vela Pulsar rotates approximately 11 times per second.
The Vela Pulsar is a neutron star formed during a supernova explosion of a massive star.
The supernova explosion that created the Vela Pulsar occurred roughly 10,000 to 11,000 years ago.
The Vela Pulsar is approximately 12 miles (20 kilometers) in diameter.
The Vela Pulsar is located approximately 1,000 light-years away from Earth.
A pulsar glitch is a sudden, abrupt increase in its rotational spin speed.
Glitches in the Vela Pulsar occur unpredictably roughly once every three years.
Astronomers recorded a Vela Pulsar glitch live in action for the first time using a radio telescope.
The radio telescope used to capture the live glitch was located at the Mount Pleasant Radio Observatory in Tasmania.
Right as the glitch occurred, the pulsar missed a single pulse, or nulled.
The spin-up glitch process took approximately five seconds to occur.
Pulsar glitches are theorized to occur when the faster superfluid core transfers rotational speed to the slower outer crust.
Radiation emissions reaching 20 teraelectronvolts (TeV) have been detected from the Vela Pulsar.
The Vela Pulsar emits jets of high-velocity charged particles streaming outwards along its rotation axis.

disputed: Distance measurements vary slightly across sources: NASA and popular science sources state 1,000 light-years, Wikipedia states ~800 light-years, and HST parallax studies state ~294 parsecs (~960 light-years). Script should state 'roughly 1,000 light-years away'.
Neutron star mass is cited as ~1.4 solar masses in S4 and ~1.5 solar masses in S5. Script should describe it as 'about 1.4 to 1.5 times the mass of our Sun'.
